title: Mikel Arteta’s New Arsenal Contract Is a Reward for the Money He’s Owed
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Grey Whitebloom7:30 AM EDTMikel Arteta is the longest serving manager in English soccer. / James Gill/Danehouse/Getty Images“The vast majority of papers out there say coaches don’t matter,” AC Milan’s data-led former co-owner Luke Bornn once said, presumably out of earshot of San Siro’s dugout. “I’m oversimplifying, but that’s basically it.”

Soccer is a sport which willfully defies statistical analysis. This is a game played with a round ball and the blunt instrument of the human foot on an open field filled with 22 charging bodies. Finding a way to parse that chaos in a spreadsheet has been an ongoing battle for decades.

One of the major breakthroughs was the discovery that a club’s salary bill offered a closer indication of a team’s quality in the long run than almost anything else. It’s an intuitive concept: in the ultimate meritocracy that is competitive sport, the best are often paid the most.

However, as Simon Kuper and Stefan Szymanski note in their seminal historical analysis, Soccernomics, “Player wages’ don’t explain everything about league position—merely almost everything at most clubs. That leaves room for a few good managers to make a difference.”

Mikel Arteta is one of those “few good managers.” His greatest success—and arguably his greatest failure—is that far too many people forget the relative imbalance he has overcome at Arsenal. As the hierarchy in north London have proven with his lucrative new contract, they, at least, are aware of his value.

Mikel Arteta has led Arsenal into the top two in each of the past four seasons. / David Price/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesWhen it looked as though Arsenal were faltering towards a fourth consecutive second-place finish last season, it was almost universally accepted that to miss out on the title to Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City yet again would have been a gross failure for Arteta. The Basque boss himself subscribed to that theory, losing countless nights of sleep to the prospect of history repeating itself.
However, even if Arsenal had slipped to second, it would still have represented a gross over-performance when compared to their position in the financial landscape of the Premier League.

Between the 2022–23 and 2025–26 seasons, Arsenal collected more top-flight points than any other team in the division (narrowly outstripping Manchester City 332 to 329). Yet, across the same span, the Gunners only ranked fifth for money spent on their wage bill.
* Data compiled from official club accounts and valuball’s estimate of the 2025–26 figures.

So, rather than consistently fighting for the title, an average coach would have been expected to skirt around the fringes of Champions League qualification with Arsenal’s wage bill. Throughout Arteta’s entire tenure in north London, the Gunners have never been blessed with the most expensively assembled roster of talent.

This is a consequence of the sort of strict salary control adopted by Daniel Levy across the road at Tottenham Hotspur. Yet, while the revolving door of dramatically contrasting Spurs coaches constantly railed against the restrictions put on the club’s ambition, Arteta simply set about improving what he had been given.
Arteta didn’t always sulk quietly through transfer windows. Back in January 2025, he fretted over Arsenal’s “certain limitations” in the market.
“Compared to what other clubs have done in terms of spending, we are really out of touch.”
Later that month, Arteta claimed that he had been left with “one of the thinnest squads in the league.”

Arsenal can scarcely be accused of not matching their manager’s ambition: Since the roster was rejuvenated with a youthful burst of players in 2021 the wage bill has increased each year. The Gunners simply haven’t surpassed the inflation of the Premier League, whose clubs all spend more each season.

Now Arsenal boast the deepest pool of talent in the division, if not across Europe. Yet, Arteta hasn’t been given a blank checkbook. After the close of this summer’s transfer window, the club’s roster cost them $1.15 billion to assemble, which is only the fifth most expensive squad in the Premier League. Alongside some savvy acquisitions, Arteta’s coaching has helped close that perception gap.

Arsenal spend like a team which should be competing with Aston Villa while rivaling Manchester City but Arteta rarely elicits more praise than Unai Emery, let alone the regal figure of Pep Guardiola. That, in part, is his own doing.

Arteta is an easy target. This is a character who let Amazon Prime’s cameras film him preparing his team for a trip to Liverpool’s inhospitable Anfield home by training in front of speakers blaring out crowd noise. They were thumped 4–0. Arteta has hired pickpockets, professional freestylers and bought the squad a dog. Only recently, he freely admitted to deliberately disrupting matchday travel plans to keep his players on their toes in the event of a real-world delay.
The gimmicks aren’t Arteta’s issue, it’s his transparency.
